title: Acidity of Phenols
page_title: Acidity of Phenols - A level Chemistry Revision Notes

blocks.md:
- Although phenol compounds contain an **alcohol **(-OH) group, they are **weakly acidic**
- This is due to the **delocalisation** of one of the lone pairs from the oxygen atom into the aromatic ring
- This increases the electron density of the ring and increases the acidic behaviour

- The **conjugate base **of phenol is the **phenoxide ion**
- In the phenoxide ion, the **negative charge **on the oxygen is spread out over the entire ion
- This is possible as **one of the lone pairs **on the oxygen atom **overlaps **with the delocalised π system of the ring
- Because of this delocalisation, there is less **charge density **on the oxygen atom
- The H<sup>+</sup> ions are therefore not strongly **attracted **to the phenoxide ion and are less likely to **reform **the **phenol **molecule
- This means that phenol is more likely to **lose **a proton (and act as an **acid**) rather than to **gain **a proton (and act as a **base** )

blocks.text: The equilibrium between phenol and the phenoxide ion

blocks.alt: Hydroxy Compounds - Delocalisation in Phenol, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes

blocks.md: ***The negative charge is spread over the ion, causing the electrons to become less available for bonding with an incoming proton***

- Phenol **ionises **to form a **more stable **negative **phenoxide **ion with its negative charge **spread out**
- This means that phenol is **more likely **to undergo **ionisation**
- The equilibrium position, therefore, lies further to the **right **and a higher proportion of phenol molecules **donate **a **proton **compared to for example water and ethanol
- The phenol compound is, therefore, more likely to act as an **acid **rather than a base

- Therefore, the position of equilibrium lies:

  - Further to the **right-hand side** favouring the **dissociated phenoxide ions**
  - Further to the **left-hand side **favouring the **undissociated ethoxide and hydroxide ions**

blocks.md: ***Since the phenoxide ion formed from the ionisation of phenol is more stable than phenol itself, the equilibrium position lies further to the right-hand-side and phenol is more likely to act as an acid rather than a base***

blocks.name: Relative Acidities of Water, Phenol & Ethanol

blocks.text: Relative Acidities of Water, Phenol & Ethanol

blocks.md:
- The p*K*<sub>*a*</sub> is a measure of the acidity of a substance
- The values of water, phenol, and ethanol show that phenol is a **stronger **acid than ethanol and water

blocks.text: Relative acidity of ethanol, water & phenol table

blocks.md:
| **Acid** | **Dissociation** | **p*****K***<sub>**a**</sub>** at 25 **<sup>**o**</sup>**C** |
|---|---|---|
| **Ethanol** | C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (aq) $\rightleftharpoons$ C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>–</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) | 16 |
| **Water** | H<sub>2</sub>O (l) $\rightleftharpoons$ OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) | 14 |
| **Phenol** | C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (aq) $\rightleftharpoons$ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>–</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) | 10 |
- The order of acidity can be explained by looking at their **conjugate** **bases** which are formed from the dissociation of the compounds

- In the **phenoxide ion** (which is the conjugate base of phenol) the charge density on the oxygen atom is **spread out **over the entire ion
- As a result, the electrons on the oxygen atom are **less available **for bond formation with a proton (H<sup>+</sup> ion)
- The **conjugate base **of ethanol is the **ethoxide ion**
- The **ethyl **group in the ion is an **electron-donating **group that donates electron density to the oxygen atom
- As a result, the electron density on the oxygen atom is **more readily available **for bond formation with a H<sup>+</sup> ion

blocks.text: The equilibrium between ethanol and the ethanoate ion

blocks.alt: Hydroxy Compounds - Ethoxide Ion, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes

blocks.md: ***The electron-donating alkyl group in the ethoxide ion concentrates charge density on the oxygen atom which can more easily bond an H***<sup>***+***</sup>*** ion***

- The **conjugate base **of water is the **hydroxide ion**
- Since the charge density of the oxygen atom cannot become delocalised over a ring, the hydroxide ion more readily accepts an H<sup>+</sup> ion compared to the phenoxide ion

  - Water is, therefore, a **stronger base **compared to phenol
- However, as there are no **electron-donating **alkyl groups, less negative charge is concentrated on the oxygen atom which therefore less readily accepts an H<sup>+</sup> ion compared to the ethoxide ion

  - Water is, therefore, a **weaker base **compared to ethanol

blocks.text: The equilibrium between water and the hydroxide ion

blocks.alt: Hydroxy Compounds - Hydroxide Ion, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes

blocks.md: ***The hydroxide ion lacks an aromatic ring and electron-donating alkyl groups so water is a stronger base than phenol but a weaker base than ethanol***

- Therefore, the position of equilibrium lies:

  - Further to the **right-hand side** favouring the **dissociated phenoxide ions**
  - Further to the **left-hand side **favouring the **undissociated ethoxide and hydroxide ions**
